name: git remote
shortDescription: Manage the set of tracked remote repositories. Remotes are named URLs that point to copies of your repository hosted elsewhere.
detailedDescription:
A remote in Git is a bookmark for another copy of your repository — usually hosted on a service like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. The `git remote` command lets you create, view, rename, and delete these bookmarks.

When you `git clone`, a remote named `origin` is automatically created pointing to the source URL. Most projects only need this one remote, but you can have multiple — for example, `upstream` pointing to the original repo when working on a fork.

Remotes don't automatically sync. They're just URLs. You use `git fetch`, `git pull`, and `git push` to transfer data between your local repo and the remote.

parameters.description: Show URLs along with remote names. Displays both fetch and push URLs (they can differ).
Create a new remote with the given name and URL.
Remove a remote and all its tracking branches and config.
Rename a remote. All remote-tracking branches are updated automatically.
Change the URL of an existing remote. Useful when migrating repos or switching from HTTPS to SSH.
Display detailed information about a remote: URL, HEAD branch, tracked branches, and push/pull configuration.

examples.title: List configured remotes
examples.description: See all remotes and their URLs.
examples.code:
git remote -v

# Output:
# origin  https://github.com/you/project.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/you/project.git (push)

examples.title: Add an upstream remote (fork workflow)
examples.description: When working on a fork, add the original repo as 'upstream' to pull updates from it.
examples.code:
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original/project.git

# Now sync with the original repo:
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

examples.title: Switch from HTTPS to SSH
examples.description: Change a remote's URL to use SSH instead of HTTPS (avoids password prompts).
examples.code:
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:you/project.git

# Verify:
git remote -v

examples.title: Get detailed remote info
examples.description: See everything Git knows about a remote.
examples.code:
git remote show origin

# Shows: fetch/push URLs, HEAD branch, remote branches,
# local branches configured for pull/push, stale branches

commonMistakes.text: Removing a remote (`git remote remove`) deletes all its tracking branches locally. The remote repository itself is NOT affected — it still exists on the server.
`origin` is just a convention name — it's not special. You can rename it to anything. But most tools and docs assume `origin`, so keeping it avoids confusion.
